title: Hera's Wednesday Dimorphos Asteroid Images Will Test Three Conflicting DART Crater Forecasts
excerpt: Hera Dimorphos images arrive Wednesday, Nov. 25, when ESA livestreams the first close-up views of the asteroid moon NASA’s DART hit in 2022. content:
ESA will livestream the first close-up images from its Hera spacecraft of the asteroid moon Dimorphos at 1:45 p.m. ET on Wednesday, Nov. 25, and the pictures will start answering a question that ESA's own published materials answer three different ways: did NASA's 2022 DART impact leave a crater, or did it reshape the entire body? The answer reaches past the picture itself, because Sabina Raducan, who led the reshaping simulations, said part of the 33-minute orbit change would be due to the change in the asteroid's shape.

Hera has arrived at its target asteroids, so Wednesday's broadcast is the first chance to compare what the spacecraft sees against forecasts made before anyone had looked. Nothing about the Didymos pair threatens Earth, because neither asteroid poses an impact threat before or after DART's test. The stakes are scientific and practical for planetary defense, because future deflection planning depends on what this mission measures.

Livestream Runs 1:45 to 2:30 p.m. ET Wednesday From Berlin Museum's Dinosaur Hall

ESA will broadcast from the dinosaur hall of Berlin's Museum für Naturkunde from 1:45 to 2:30 p.m. ET (19:45 to 20:30 CET), according to ESA's livestream announcement, and says viewers can follow on ESA WebTV and ESA's YouTube channel. Newsweek reports the same date.

ESA also plans to point viewers to hera.esa.int, where it describes the Hera Space Companion as a mission-linked communication platform rather than just an AI chatbot.

ESA Models Disagree: Sizable Crater or Reshaped Moonlet

Three published forecasts for Dimorphos's surface do not agree.

The first comes from Hubble. After DART's impact, astronomers counted boulders drifting away from Dimorphos, and UCLA's David Jewitt said the boulders could come from a circle about 160 feet (about 50 m) across. That figure marks where the boulders likely came from, not a measured crater, and NASA's release says Hera will eventually determine the actual crater size.

The second sits on ESA's mission page for the target asteroid, which says DART's impact was modeled to have possibly left a sizable crater on the scale of 20 m (about 66 ft) in diameter.

The third points the other way. Simulations by Raducan and colleagues in Nature Astronomy found, in ESA's 2024 summary of the study, that "the crater grew to encompass the entire body itself," so Hera would probably find no distinct DART crater. The team estimated that about 1% of Dimorphos's mass was thrown into space and about 8% shifted around the body. The simulations treat Dimorphos as a weak rubble pile covered in boulders.

Hera's own science team has not picked a side. In a July abstract for the Europlanet Science Congress, team members including Patrick Michel and Michael Küppers framed the open question as whether a crater exists or Dimorphos was entirely reshaped, and said they are confident Hera's images will have little similarity with the pre-impact pictures DART returned.

Pixel Math Limits What Wednesday's Images Can Say About Crater Size

Hera's Asteroid Framing Camera records 1020 by 1020 pixels across a 5.5-degree field of view, with each pixel spanning 94.1 microradians. Multiply by distance and the pixel size follows. These are TechTimes calculations from the published specifications, not ESA figures.

The first-light image in mid-October came from about 1,280 km (795 miles), where each pixel covers roughly 120 m (395 ft). Dimorphos, about 151 m (495 ft) across on average, filled about one pixel in that image.

If Wednesday's images come from Hera's current standoff of 25 to 30 km (15.5 to 18.6 miles), each pixel covers about 2.4 to 2.8 m (7.7 to 9.3 ft). At 28.5 km (17.7 miles), Dimorphos would span about 56 pixels, a 20 m (66 ft) crater about 7 to 8 pixels, and a roughly 50 m (164 ft) boulder-source patch about 19 pixels. That would likely be enough to flag a depression or its absence, but too coarse to measure rim shape or depth. ESA has not said what range Wednesday's images come from.

ESA aims for resolution better than 10 cm (3.9 in) near the impact site, which would require a range of about 1.06 km (0.66 miles).

Safety-First Rectangular Orbits Keep Hera Far From Dimorphos for Now

Hera cannot simply orbit Dimorphos like a satellite around Earth. Gravity at Didymos is about 40,000 times weaker than Earth's and about 200,000 times weaker at Dimorphos, so ESA flies Hera in "rectangular orbits" at 25 to 30 km (15.5 to 18.6 miles): nearly straight lines at about 12 cm/s (4.7 in/s), with thruster firings on a cycle of three days and then four, each turning the course by 90 degrees.

The design trades resolution for safety. If a thruster firing fails, ESA says, Hera drifts away rather than risking collision. That is why the closest views, and the sharpest look at any scar, come later in the mission. ESA's rectangular-orbit page says Hera "will reveal which forecast was the correct one," adding "if any."

Didymos Views So Far Show a Sharp Ridge and Boulders, Not Dimorphos Detail

DLR, the German Aerospace Center and scientific lead for the camera, published images of Didymos on Nov. 12 and added further visible, thermal-infrared and multispectral views on Nov. 17, including views taken from about 28.5 km (17.7 miles). They show the larger asteroid's sharp equatorial ridge and large surface boulders.

Those views say little about Dimorphos's surface. ESA bills Wednesday's livestream as Hera's first images of post-impact Dimorphos.

When Will Hera Move Closer, and Will Its CubeSats Land on Dimorphos?

ESA plans bowtie-shaped hyperbolic arcs from about 20 km (12.4 miles) in December, and over the coming months Hera will deploy the CubeSats Milani and Juventas, with landing described as a later step. The investigation is planned to run at least six months from November.

Pictures alone will not settle how efficiently DART pushed Dimorphos. Researchers reported that the impact shortened Dimorphos's orbit by about 33 minutes and put the momentum enhancement factor near 3.61, called beta, within a plausible range of 2.2 to 4.9 across assumed densities. Pinning beta down requires Dimorphos's mass, which ESA says Hera will measure by observing the wobble of Didymos. Wednesday's images tell scientists what Dimorphos looks like; the mass measurement will tell them how efficiently DART pushed it.

If Hera's views show no crater and a reshaped body, that would match the weak rubble-pile picture in the Raducan simulations. A distinct crater of the modeled size would be a result those simulations did not expect. Either answer sharpens the planning for the next time humanity needs to move an asteroid.

Frequently Asked Questions

When and where can I watch ESA's Hera livestream of Dimorphos?

ESA will stream it live from 1:45 to 2:30 p.m. ET on Wednesday, Nov. 25 (19:45 to 20:30 CET) from the dinosaur hall of Berlin's Museum für Naturkunde, per ESA's livestream announcement. Viewers can follow on ESA WebTV and ESA's YouTube channel.

Did DART leave a crater on Dimorphos?

Nobody knows yet. ESA's published materials range from a sizable crater about 66 feet across to no crater at all because the whole moonlet was reshaped, and Hera's team lists crater versus reshaping as open. The answer matters because Raducan said part of the 33-minute orbit change would be due to a change in shape.

Will Wednesday's images show how well DART deflected Dimorphos?

Not by themselves. Images reveal shape and surface, while deflection efficiency depends on Dimorphos's mass, which ESA says Hera will measure by observing the wobble of Didymos.

Do Didymos or Dimorphos threaten Earth?

No. NASA says neither asteroid poses an impact threat to Earth, before or after DART's kinetic impact demonstration.
